speakers: Katie Kaminski (guest co-host, trend-following researcher; author of the 'crisis or correction' paper)
summary: Systematic Investor 344 (April 2025): Niels and Katie Kaminski analyse trend following during the tariff shock using her paper 'Trade War: Crisis or Correction?'. Conclusions: trend typically loses in the first phase of equity drawdowns under ~15 percent and earns crisis alpha only in deeper or longer ones; dispersion between managers is normal after shocks; speed, market universe, correlation and volatility handling drive differences; return stacking creates a new portfolio construction problem.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: these terrorists were much bigger than than they expected and that this was really making their job um pretty uh difficult.
claims.claim: Fed Chair Powell said tariffs were much bigger than expected, creating tension in the dual mandate and effectively putting the Fed on hold.
claims.conditions: tariff shock raises inflation and growth risks

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: I certainly don't think it would help the situation if someone like a J Jerome Powell uh was somehow ousted from the Fed.
claims.claim: Removing Powell from the Fed would worsen the turmoil.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: long gold apparently is the most crowded trade according to their survey.
claims.claim: The Bank of America fund manager survey (April 2025) shows long gold has replaced the Magnificent 7 as the most crowded trade, and CTAs are also long gold.
claims.indicator: BofA Global Fund Manager Survey most crowded trade

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: it's been mostly the financial sectors that have been causing uh the problems like equities uh like currencies
claims.claim: In April 2025 trend losses came mostly from equities and currencies, with no usual offset from fixed income.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: we haven't had much offset in say fixed income that you know often happens.
claims.claim: Fixed income did not offset the equity selloff as it usually does in risk-off episodes.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the JGBs because that really got a short squeeze um uh in in the last couple of weeks
claims.claim: JGB futures produced trouble for CTAs through a short squeeze in April 2025.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: another part part of the portfolio which is usually uh something we can rely on if we are positioned correctly and that is the short-term interest rates.
claims.claim: Short-term interest rate positions, along with gold and energies, were bright spots in April 2025, though not universal across countries (Europe strongest).

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: you have this scenario where equities sell off aggressively and in that same scenario yields went up and the dollar sold off.
claims.claim: In the tariff shock equities fell while yields rose and the dollar fell, unlike the usual safe-haven response, indicating vulnerability in US assets and a possibly new regime for bonds and the dollar.
claims.conditions: tariff shock; flight from US assets
claims.testable: yes: event study of dollar and yields on equity drops

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: as the trends shift quickly, depending on where you're standing before they fall, that's going to impact how you perform until you can adjust to where the new trends and the new macro developments are.
claims.claim: When trends shift quickly, performance depends on prior positioning until the system adjusts to the new trends.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: even if you cut rates on the short end If inflation comes in because of this, then you have, you know, the potential for a huge steepener
claims.claim: Bonds are hard to trade: foreign selling of US assets plus tariff inflation could cause a huge curve steepener even if short-end rates are cut.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: what happened actually had the opposite effect at least in the short term where you saw that the dollar actually has lost some competitive advantage
claims.claim: Tariff policy aimed at fixing trade imbalances should have been dollar-positive but instead the dollar lost ground, raising questions about its key-currency role.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: trend longer term can pick up a real seismic shift in policy not sort of a a freef fall
claims.claim: Trend following over longer horizons can capture a real policy-driven regime shift, as opposed to a free fall.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: This is where it doesn't feel comfortable getting in but this is historically exactly where you want to get in.
claims.claim: After a CTA drawdown that feels uncomfortable, historically is exactly when to allocate.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: how we were positioned going into this
claims.claim: CTAs lost money in the shock because of how they were positioned before it, not because of the market move itself.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: Stocken trend down 6.48 uh down uh 10.84 for the year.
claims.claim: In mid-April 2025 BTOP50 was -5.26, SG CTA -8.36, SG Trend -10.84 percent YTD, versus the S&P 500 total return -9.95 percent, MSCI World -6.5 percent and US aggregate bonds +2 percent; trend barometer 45.
claims.indicator: BTOP50, SG CTA, SG Trend, trend barometer

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: So definitely doing better in the short-term time frames.
claims.claim: The short-term traders index was only about -1 percent in April 2025 and flat on the year, outperforming trend in the shock.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: when the S&P 500 moves 1% that's sort of like a one sigma move. So if you move 10% that's a 10 sigma move like approximately.
claims.claim: Counting S&P moves in sigmas (1 percent is about one sigma) gauges how intense a shock is.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: how does managed futures do across different draw downs for the S&P 500 peak to trroth across different dimensions
claims.claim: Katie's paper 'Trade War: Crisis or Correction?' measures managed futures returns across S&P 500 peak-to-trough drawdowns by depth and length.
claims.indicator: SG CTA/managed futures index vs S&P drawdown depth and duration

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: anything less than 15% actually tends to be negative.
claims.claim: For S&P drawdowns under about 15 percent trend following tends to lose.
claims.indicator: trend returns in S&P drawdowns less than 15%

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: when markets get a shock, it's often in the opposite direction of current prevailing trends in various orders of magnitude depending on what's going on.
claims.claim: Shocks usually run against prevailing trends, so trend must adjust and is often on the wrong side initially.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: the first part of the draw down is often a negative environment for trend following. And as you move farther down, you know, deeper drawdowns and longer draw downs, that's where you see, you know, that type of crisis alpha
claims.claim: Trend is negative early in a drawdown and generates crisis alpha (second responder) in deeper and longer ones such as the tech bubble, GFC and 2022.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: we don't really chase the the sell-off, but we ride that unraveling that happens in the in the slipstream of of the selloff
claims.claim: Trend followers do not chase the selloff but ride the unravelling that follows it.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: I divided those into two sections. One was short sharp draw downs and the other was extended crisis periods.
claims.claim: Deep drawdown episodes are split into short sharp recoveries and extended crises to compare trend paths.
claims.indicator: trend path in short sharp vs extended drawdowns

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: it actually looks a lot like the start of the tech bubble.
claims.claim: The 2025 episode so far (20 to 30 days) resembles the start of the tech bubble (500 plus days), where trend initially struggled but later did very well, so a larger story may be ahead if recession or inflation develops.
claims.indicator: trend path vs S&P drawdown analogs

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: short sharp draw downs that actually recover and you have a few of those. You have 2018 and you also have 2020
claims.claim: In short sharp recovering drawdowns (2018 and 2020) trend behaved like in the first weeks of 2025.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: he divided up the draw down of how does CTAs typically react when you have a 10% the first 10% of an S&P draw down and then how what happens once you get from 10 to 20.
claims.claim: A chart by Tyler Lovingood splits CTA performance in the first 10 percent of an S&P drawdown versus from 10 to 20 percent.
claims.indicator: CTA performance by S&P drawdown stage

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the draw down of the S&P close to close was 18.7.
claims.claim: From the Feb 19 high to the Apr 8 low the S&P fell 18.7 percent while SG CTA fell 8.6 and SG Trend 10.76 percent, so trend had not turned positive before the 20 percent level.
claims.indicator: S&P drawdown, SG CTA, SG Trend

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: I would almost classify this as chaos not necessarily crisis
claims.claim: Niels suggests there could be different shocks, chaos vs crisis, requiring different alpha solutions.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: crisis alpha is is not a guarantee. It's just this idea of how do you try to find strategies that might be able to do well in different crisises.
claims.claim: Crisis alpha is a search for strategies that may do well in different crises, not a guarantee, and different crises need different tools.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: they talk about the first responder the second responders and third responders and you got to think about building a portfolio with attributes utes that might be able to catch it.
claims.claim: The Makita first/second/third responder framework: build a portfolio with attributes that catch different phases of a crisis rather than one tool.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: It's often volatility strategies or other types of approaches and sometimes it's even cash you know.
claims.claim: Chaos or crisis alpha can come from volatility strategies or even cash.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: a lot of people would have classified long US treasuries in the first responder group and of course this time that didn't work either.
claims.claim: Long US Treasuries, a classic first responder, also failed in April 2025, showing classifications give no guarantee.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: if you think about a very extreme market environment like what we experience or like co so much matters how where are you standing before you fall
claims.claim: In extreme shocks return dispersion across trend managers is wide because outcomes depend on position size and direction before the shock, much like coin tosses.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: if you held more European equities than someone else, if you had short signals instead of long signals, even marginal differences there, you had big differences in return over those days
claims.claim: Small differences in positions such as European equity exposure or signal direction produced big return differences in the shock days.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: We try to aggregate multiple different approaches for how we measure trends. We try to incorporate risk management to adjust for changing volatility.
claims.claim: Managers reduce dispersion risk by aggregating several trend measures and adjusting for changing volatility, though shocks remain unpredictable.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the difference between having a you know 100 day moving average and 105day moving average in that one particular year was like 20% performance difference
claims.claim: A paper showed a 100-day vs 105-day moving average could differ by about 20 percent in one year, so parameter choice can drive large short-run differences.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: they will admit that yeah they were lucky this time around
claims.claim: Replicator providers admit they were lucky to be fast enough in the 2025 shock; performance goes in cycles.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: in that bond trade some managers got that better than others and you know it just had to do with how they designed their systems
claims.claim: In 2022 the bond trend result differed across managers because of system design.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: having very simple parameters can create more return dispersions that's why managers have learned to kind of you know build robust signal processes that combine different methodologies and approaches
claims.claim: Simple single-parameter implementations create more return dispersion, so robust managers diversify parameters and methods.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: even something like whether you have static position sizing or dynamic position sizing will make a very big difference.
claims.claim: Static versus dynamic position sizing makes a big difference in short crisis periods; dynamic worked in the last two or three years but is painful at turns.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: it's trading speed, it's the universe of markets and how you weight them, and it's the risk management.
claims.claim: What differentiates one trend engine from another is trading speed, market universe and weights, and risk management.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: adding trend following to your portfolio to your your full portfolio uh is just such a easy decision to make quote unquote because um you know you can improve your upside you can reduce your downside
claims.claim: Adding trend to a full portfolio can improve upside and reduce downside, motivating return-stacking products (Standpoint, Cory Hoffstein).

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: we have seen a consistent shift to slower trend systems and you know that makes sense you know trading costs and also capturing sort of long-term risk premia
claims.claim: The trend industry has consistently shifted to slower systems, reflecting trading costs and the capture of long-term risk premia, which worked until recently.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: if you are only in longer term trading speeds your ability to pivot especially if it's a longer dislocation is going to be less uh possible.
claims.claim: Slow-only systems cannot pivot in dislocations, so some reactivity helps capture crises.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: if you're leaning into long-term risk premier, you're looking a lot more like equities
claims.claim: Leaning into slow, long-term risk premia makes trend look like equities and lowers diversification.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: shorter term trend systems have a lower sharp, especially more recently, but they have that diversification characteristics that can help
claims.claim: Shorter-term trend has lower Sharpe recently but better diversification, which helps when added to equities.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: the cost effectiveness in terms of margining and the collateral efficiency that the futures markets provide so that you can actually get that 200% exposure
claims.claim: Futures margin makes portable alpha capital efficient, allowing 150 to 200 percent exposure without more money.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: when you combine those two your new objective can become a little different because now you're doing a portfolio construction problem
claims.claim: Combining equities and trend changes the objective: it becomes a portfolio construction and rebalancing problem rather than standalone best Sharpe.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: when you combine equities and trend they're naturally very cohesive but you know that problem of how do you balance them over time is something that investors do struggle with
claims.claim: Equities and trend combine well, but balancing them over time is hard; rebalancing exploits their relation and makes the holding more holdable.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: just put them together which is a classic portable alpha or we can kind of start to say you know there are smart ways to think about risk management of those two things.
claims.claim: Instead of naive portable alpha stacking, risk-manage equities and trend jointly.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: whenever you want to specialize your view instead of diversification, you need to look for statistical evidence and you need to adjust your view as a function of the level of statistical evidence.
claims.claim: Tilting trend speed by asset class has little statistical evidence and should be done only on the margin; there is no magic speed.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: that's pretty consistent with this philosophical idea is you never know where the next trend may be.
claims.claim: Be agnostic across markets: precious metals, industrial metals or cocoa were dismissed for decades but trended when macro conditions changed; the signal should decide when to trade.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: in certain environments you see where those global macro trends are really the big driver of a lot of trend performance
claims.claim: Sometimes global macro trends (2022 fixed income) drive most performance, other times idiosyncratic markets add diversification.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: soybeans for example, right, have gone up really a lot.
claims.claim: In April 2025 soybeans rose while energy and many commodities fell, showing diversification from idiosyncratic trends.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: makes it harder to work out for investors how good is the alpha engine.
claims.claim: A single combined return stream in portable alpha hides how good the trend engine is, so its contribution should be tracked.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: if there's one thing that probably unites us in terms of when we want to trade, it's actually adjustment for volatility in the position sizing
claims.claim: Volatility adjustment in position sizing is the shared trigger that makes trend managers trade at the same time.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: if they're trading based on inflation or rising rates they have positive correlation which means that if you're long both of them at the same time you have more risk on.
claims.claim: When stocks and bonds are driven by inflation or rates they are positively correlated, so being long both is more risk and correlation is needed to see where the risk is.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: in the first part of this selloff, you were registering positive correlation between US assets and equities and then later on that actually flipped.
claims.claim: Correlation between US assets and equities was positive early in the April 2025 selloff and then flipped, showing correlation is volatile.
claims.indicator: correlation of US assets with equities

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: suddenly you're in a world where correlations do matter and change a lot
claims.claim: After 2020 fixed income became vulnerable (inflation, US assets), so correlations matter more and must be incorporated, with skepticism about their volatility.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: if you just assume that stocks and bonds have negative correlation and you pile into both of them and you have a risk model that has a long-term estimate for correlation
claims.claim: A risk model with a long-term negative stock-bond correlation underestimates risk when the correlation turns positive.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: they don't have any assumption about they just say here's my entry and here's my stop and that's it and I don't need to worry about it.
claims.claim: Some CTAs ignore correlation and use entries and stops, which still exposes them but protects with stops.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: correlation by the way is not something you can measure over short-term periods with success I think you need to give it a bit of time
claims.claim: Correlation cannot be measured reliably over short windows, so being too precise on correlations in chaotic periods may not help.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: currencies have a volatility, let's say the yen around 10%, and then commodities have a volatility around 40%. So guess what? You need like a ratio of 4:1.
claims.claim: Position sizing by volatility balances risk across assets (10 percent vol currencies vs 40 percent commodities means 4:1), like risk parity.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: in the year of you know 2022 when bond vault was 2x
claims.claim: When bond volatility doubled in 2022 volatility sizing forced trend to rethink risk per asset.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: in any sort of signal generation you have to look at how much signal do I have versus the noise and so intrinsically in how strong the trend is defined is always the volatility measure
claims.claim: Volatility enters signal strength as signal-to-noise as well as position sizing.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: even if you know the volatility it doesn't improve your performance that much.
claims.claim: Even perfect volatility foresight barely improves trend performance because volatility gives the range not the direction.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: How much do you incorporate shocks, jumps into your estimation
claims.claim: The practical vol-estimation question is how much to include shocks and jumps, as in the nickel event.
